text: now that treams-rs is published, i want to look into making it faster, including reviving the old gpu branch (but really any other method of making it faster too). investigate and tell me where you think the biggest gains may lie

items.html:
I’d prioritize translation work and solver algorithms, while reviving the GPU code selectively. The largest broad gains appear to come from reusing calculations and reducing all-pairs work. The old GPU branch has a credible win for repeated field sampling, but doesn’t establish a general acceleration of scattering solves.

I inspected current main, the GPU branch, and archived benchmarks, then ran four fresh release-build benchmarks.

1. Large clusters: the strongest overall opportunity

The matrix-free solver regenerates every particle-pair translation on every GMRES iteration. It also solves incident-field columns separately, repeating those translations across illuminations. These are concrete costs in the current implementation.

Fresh measurements on the Ryzen 9950X, four pinned cores, complex128, weakly scattering spheres at lmax=1:

Spheres Illuminations Matrix-free fresh solve Selected LU fresh solve
128 1 8.8 ms 12.2 ms
128 8 66.5 ms 12.7 ms
512 1 156.7 ms 283.3 ms
1,024 1 625.2 ms Not measured

Eight illuminations cost 7.5× as much as one in matrix-free mode. Doubling from 512 to 1,024 particles costs 4×, with six GMRES iterations in both cases. The expensive part is the pairwise work, rather than worsening convergence. Run details and results

I’d investigate, in this order:

  • Batched operator applications across illuminations, sharing translations between right-hand sides.
  • Reusable translation data, with an explicit memory budget. Caching every full block would sacrifice much of matrix-free’s memory advantage; smaller radial/harmonic tables are another option.
  • Neighbour-block preconditioning and warm starts for strongly coupled systems and parameter sweeps. The present weak cases already converge quickly, so preconditioning alone won’t transform these timings.
  • FMM or hierarchical interaction compression for genuinely large clusters. This is the most plausible route to order-of-magnitude gains as particle count grows, because it attacks quadratic work. Fast multipole acceleration has been demonstrated for electromagnetic superposition T-matrix methods, including nonspherical constituents. It would require substantial numerical and analytic-gradient work here. Relevant paper

A GPU pairwise kernel could complement these changes. The old branch does not contain that implementation.

2. GPU revival: worthwhile, with a narrower first target

The branch’s historical RTX 4080 SUPER measurements are informative:

Path Historical gain Important boundary
Repeated application of a cached plane-field operator 6.4–7.5× through Python Fixed geometry; substantial setup and storage
Fused plane-field evaluation 1.5–2.8× Avoids storing the full operator
Dense complex128 LU, dimension 4,096 and 64 RHS 1.14× Near parity
Reused resident LU solve, same shape 0.82× GPU slower

The cached-field comparison included CPU caching and a prepared fused CPU alternative, so this wasn’t simply caching on one side. However, the two large Python cases required an estimated 86–138 applications to amortize cold setup, with 384 MiB–1.5 GiB operator storage. Geometry/wavevector gradients and framework integration were absent. (Sampling evidence), dense evidence

I would port the resident matrix operations and tests onto current main, then benchmark a complete repeated-field objective and its pullback. The branch needs adaptation to current module, threading, and floating-point conventions.

There is also a useful exact simplification: cache the scalar plane-wave phase matrix and apply three component-weighted coefficient columns. That reduces cached operator storage 3×; its runtime benefit remains unmeasured.

The weak dense-LU result applies to this consumer GPU. Ada has limited FP64 throughput; a GPU designed for double precision deserves a separate experiment before dismissing GPU dense algebra. NVIDIA architecture documentation

3. Periodic arrays and high-order fields: my preferred CPU experiments

Two remaining sources of duplicated work look promising:

  • Periodic translations evaluate a separate complete Ewald sum for every harmonic. Shell geometry, phases and parts of the integral calculation could be shared across a whole harmonic table. This targets both forward calculations and expensive periodic gradients. Source
  • Spherical fields still evaluate harmonic recurrences separately for each mode, despite already sharing radial values. Complete harmonic/radial tables could reduce repeated work at higher multipole orders. The translation code already contains related machinery; field pullbacks need additional derivative support. Source

These are focused experiments with broad CPU applicability. I wouldn’t attach speedup estimates yet: substantial field and lattice optimizations already landed before publication, making older timings unsuitable as today’s baseline.

4. Preserve mathematical structure through the solve

There are narrower opportunities with large theoretical upside:

  • Axisymmetric EBCM: quadrature preserves independent azimuthal m blocks, but the documented T-matrix construction uses a dense solve. Solving those blocks independently changes the solve’s order dependence from roughly O(L⁶) to O(L⁴). That is an asymptotic opportunity, not a measured whole-workflow gain. Current example
  • Thin S-matrix illumination: its iterative path first constructs the dense product LU. Applying x − L(Ux) directly could remove cubic setup where a suitable invertibility check can be retained. Source
  • Pair symmetry: dense sphere assembly evaluates both displacement directions independently. Existing translation identities could approximately halve translation evaluations, though the total solve gains less when factorization dominates.

For optimization workloads, I’d also measure the adapter separately: JAX currently reruns the native forward record during backward, and vmap executes callbacks sequentially. Improving batching or retained numerical intermediates could matter without changing a numerical kernel. Source

My first implementation experiments would be shared translations across RHS, batched periodic harmonic evaluation, and a selective GPU sampling port. I’d pursue FMM after establishing the large-cluster workloads and accuracy targets.

The four fresh CPU cases passed their existing numerical checks. The 1,024-particle case had physical/directional-gradient checks but no same-size dense reference. I did not rerun GPU benchmarks or full CI. Source and Git state remain unchanged; the local extension is now a release build. Nothing was pushed or posted.

text: ok let’s ignore gpu and focus on cpu speedups. allen’s some time on it, you’re free to choose direction. the only thing i care about is significant speedups for user relevant workloads. spend a couple of hours on it and see how far you can get.

items.html:
After about two hours, I’ve implemented up to 12.3× CPU speedups on useful workloads.

Measured against rebuilt v0.1.0 code, using four threads on the Ryzen 9950X, over seven rounds:

Workload Before → after Speedup
512 dipole spheres, eight illuminations 1.24 s → 100 ms 12.3×
Same solve + complete analytic pullback 2.57 s → 233 ms 11.0×
Four-sphere periodic array, lmax=6, including gradient 238 ms → 112 ms 2.1×
4,096-point field map of 32 dipoles 12.2 ms → 5.2 ms 2.3×
1,024-mode internal-field solve 31.6 ms → 15.5 ms 2.0×

Field maps use prepared scattering coefficients; internal-field solves use prepared slab matrices. Single-illumination cluster solves also improved by about 2.6×.

The main changes share translations across independent GMRES solves, reuse radial/harmonic and Ewald calculations, and avoid unnecessary dense reflection products. Public APIs, precision and convergence tolerances remain unchanged.

just ci passes: 262 Rust and 6,625 Python tests. Representative performance checks also pass at 1, 16 and 32 threads, including longer rechecks of noisy cases. The main tradeoff is roughly 5–6 MiB more working memory in measured batching/periodic cases; periodic cases exceed the strict memory-growth benchmark threshold. Cross-platform performance and the full historical benchmark grid remain unverified.

The next promising target is small-matrix thread scheduling. The same 64-mode stack took 19.5 ms with 32 native threads versus 0.70 ms with four, with identical output bits. That’s a measured configuration gain; automatic scheduling remains future work.

Measurements, provenance and caveats. Changes are local and uncommitted; nothing pushed, published, or changed in PRs.

text: great, look into thread scheduling too. then, turn this work into a PR. make sure to keep all documentation up to date, and think shout maintainability and the cost of adding more code. adversarial review the changes. babysit the pr through CI and merge it, then consider publishing a new version of treams-rs
if you think this should be a new release then go ahead with that too

items.html:
Pushed and merged PR #3, then published treams-rs 0.1.1.

The installed PyPI wheels confirm:

  • 11.9× faster for 512 spheres with eight illuminations; 10.9× including the complete gradient.
  • 2.3× faster prepared field maps.
  • At a 32-thread budget, scheduling improvements deliver 9.8× for small cluster solves and 19× for the small stack workload.

Adversarial review is complete and findings were fixed. Documentation and benchmark evidence are updated. APIs, tolerances and dependencies are unchanged.

Full CI, formal verification, all 20 wheel targets, TestPyPI/PyPI installation checks and live documentation checks passed. The branch is removed; main is clean.

Performance was measured on one Ryzen Linux host; the full historical benchmark grid wasn’t rerun. Some periodic workloads use additional memory. These limits and retained regressions are documented in the performance report.
